name: Esther Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That sounds good. I'm Esther, I'm 27, and I work for a carers' cooperative, which means the carers own the company together and vote on how it's run. We mostly visit people with dementia who still live at home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It starts around eight with Mrs Kowalski, who's 84 and some mornings thinks I'm her sister, so I just go with it and we do breakfast as sisters. Most of my calls are an hour long, which is rare, because the co-op fought for longer visits. I love the slow bits, the photo albums and the songs. What wears me out is the evenings, when someone's confused and frightened and I'm the only one there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a lot of people would: the robots didn't come, now let's fix pay and staffing properly. At the co-op meeting I'd say we can stop worrying about tech and get back to arguing about the rota. Online I'd probably share a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means life carries on, which is pretty good. The co-op is solid, we've got the council contract till 2029, and there are care jobs everywhere around here. I've got about eight months of pay saved, and Tom and I are saving for a deposit on a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds and keep going to co-op meetings. Tom and I would go ahead and buy the flat next year like we planned, probably a two-bedroom near the hospital where he works as a porter. I'd maybe use the translation app a bit more with clients who've slipped back into their first language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little flat, if I'm honest, because some part of me wanted something big to happen. If AI only saves time, I'd want every saved minute spent sitting with an old woman who thinks I'm her sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the council contract runs till 2029. Does that worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, every few years there's a scare when the contract comes up. Last time a big agency bid lower and we nearly lost it. But we kept it because families wrote letters, and I think that would happen again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the deposit on the flat mean for your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would take most of what Tom and I have together, but my own eight months would stay as our safety net. We'd be fine. It's the kind of risk you take when nothing much is changing.

say: I'd say the robots **didn't come**, so let's fix **pay** and staffing properly.
At the co-op I'd joke we can go back to **arguing about the rota**.
think: Privately it's good news; the co-op holds the **council contract** till 2029.
With **eight months saved** and plenty of care jobs nearby, I feel secure.
do: Keep doing the **hour-long dementia visits** and co-op meetings.
Buy a **two-bedroom flat** near the hospital with Tom next year.
Use the **translation app** more with clients who've slipped into their first language.
feel: **Calm**, and a little flat that nothing big happened.
S0.quote: If AI only saves time, I'd want every saved minute spent sitting with an old woman who thinks I'm her sister.
fieldNote: Esther defines good care as **time**: hour-long visits, photo albums and songs.
The **contract renewal** is her one standing worry, and she trusts families to defend the co-op.
She'd take the **flat purchase** risk only because the world looks stable.

steps.text: Buy a two-bedroom flat near the hospital with Tom next year
Keep doing hour-long dementia visits for the co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should choose its own tools, not have them pushed on us by the council. I'd say it on the members' group chat and at the meeting. And I'd say any time saved goes back to the clients, that's our whole point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's fine for me, mostly. My work is sitting with people and helping them wash and eat, and that's slow to automate. The care plans and the medicine charts would go onto software, which I'd quite like if it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever training the co-op runs on the new care-plan system, once one or two others have tried it. I'd vote at the members' meeting for a rule that saved time goes into longer visits. I'd keep saving as normal and still buy the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, because I've seen how tools change workplaces. My friend at a big agency says their app now tells carers when to leave. The difference between our co-op and a big agency is who decides what to do with the time a computer saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for one or two others to try it first. Who would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joanna, probably, she's our tech person and she's already testing a voice note app. If Joanna says it's fine, I'll believe it. I'm not going to be the first one to type a client's whole history into some new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two women in our office who do scheduling and invoices. That's exactly the kind of work the card describes. As a co-op we could vote to keep them on doing something else, like family liaison, and I'd vote for that.

say: I'd say the **co-op chooses** its own tools, not the council.
I'd insist **saved time** goes back into longer visits for clients.
think: Privately it's mostly fine; **washing and sitting** with people is slow to automate.
I'd quite like **care plans** and medicine charts on software, if it works.
do: Join the co-op's **care-plan training** once colleagues like Joanna have tried it.
Vote for a rule putting saved time into **longer visits**.
Keep saving and still buy the **flat** as planned.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, having heard how apps rule carers at big agencies.
S1.quote: The difference between our co-op and a big agency is who decides what to do with the time a computer saves.
fieldNote: Esther's steady style shows clearly: she waits for colleague **Joanna** to test tools first.
Her worry is about **control of saved time**, which she sees as a co-op strength.
She'd vote to **redeploy** the scheduling and invoicing staff rather than cut them.

steps.text: Take the co-op's care-plan software training after Joanna tests it
Vote to keep office staff on as family liaison workers
Keep the flat purchase with Tom on track for next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle fairly, and the government needs to step in with income support and rules on care robots. I'd be loud about it, more than usual. I'd post that people with dementia need faces they recognise, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it hits our home twice. Thinking AI by 2028 doesn't touch my visits much, but by 2031 the robots can do the washing and lifting, and Tom's porter job is basically pushing beds, so that goes too. We'd both be out of work around the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the flat on hold immediately, that's the first thing. I'd keep my eight months and try to build it to twelve. I'd push the co-op to bid for the job of running the robots in people's homes, so at least members keep some work, and I'd vote for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Tom pushes hospital beds and I wash people with dementia, so robots doing hands-on work by 2031 means our whole household is on the same clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the co-op could bid to run the robots. Do you really believe that would work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a few of us, not all twenty-six members. Somebody has to check the robot did the job and talk to the daughter on the phone. But I can't pretend that's twenty-six jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're waiting, and she'd be relieved, she always thought we were rushing. She'd offer us her spare room, which I'd hate, but I'd keep it in mind.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and government must bring **income support** and robot rules.
I'd post that people with **dementia** need faces they recognise.
think: Privately it hits our home **twice**: my care visits and **Tom's porter job**.
By **2031** we'd both be out of work around the same time.
do: Put the **flat purchase** on hold straight away.
Build savings from **eight to twelve** months.
Push the co-op to bid for **running robots** in clients' homes.
feel: **Frightened** that both incomes run on one clock.
Grudgingly grateful for **mum's spare room** as a fallback.
S2.quote: Tom pushes hospital beds and I wash people with dementia, so robots doing hands-on work by 2031 means our whole household is on the same clock.
fieldNote: The **household angle** drives her mood: her partner's job is just as hands-on.
Her co-op idea is honest about limits: a **few jobs**, not twenty-six.
She expects the three-year robot gap to help **neither** of them much.

steps.text: Put the flat purchase with Tom on hold
Build savings from eight to twelve months of pay
Vote and campaign for a basic income and robot care rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's plan who looks after people properly. At co-op meetings I'd ask that we start planning now. Online I'd be less angry than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's the same problem with a bit of breathing room. Robots arrive around 2034, when I'm 34, and Tom and I would have had a few more years of steady pay. That's enough time to get one of us into something safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time dementia specialist diploma next year, because the families I know would pay for someone who really understands dementia even with robots around. I'd learn the co-op's software properly. And we'd keep saving, maybe buy a smaller flat in a couple of years rather than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which helps. Five years is enough time for me to become the person a family calls when the robot can't calm their mother down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dementia specialist, rather than something away from care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's what I'm good at, and dementia is where people get scared and confused, and I don't think a family will hand that over to a robot first. Maybe I'm wrong. But I'd rather bet on what I know than start again in something I don't care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Tom, what would he do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's been talking about becoming a paramedic for ages, so maybe this is the push. That's thinking and hands-on together. We'd split it, one of us studying at a time, so we always have one full wage.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so let's plan who **looks after** people properly.
At the co-op I'd ask that we **start planning** now.
think: Privately it's the same problem with **breathing room**; robots around **2034**.
That's enough time to get **one of us** into something safer.
do: Start a part-time **dementia specialist diploma** next year.
Keep saving and buy a **smaller flat** in a couple of years.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time for me to become the person a family calls when the robot can't calm their mother down.
fieldNote: Esther bets on **dementia skill** as the human edge families won't hand over first.
She and Tom would take turns **studying**, always keeping one full wage.
She says openly she **might be wrong**, which keeps her plan honest.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time dementia specialist diploma next year
Learn the co-op's care-plan software properly
Save for a smaller flat and buy in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this well, so let's make sure carers and families are part of designing it. I'd volunteer for a council working group if there was one. That's the kind of thing I'd actually say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay. Robots for hands-on work by about 2039 means I'd be 40, and by then I'd hope to be a dementia specialist or running part of the co-op. Ten years is long enough to change careers twice if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead and buy the flat with Tom, because ten years of steady pay is enough to pay a lot of it down. I'd do the dementia diploma, but not in a rush, maybe in a couple of years. I'd keep my rounds and keep using the translation app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly okay. With ten years of warning I'd still buy the flat, still do the diploma, and still sing the old songs with my clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join any group about it, given ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the union or the co-op federation set something up, I'd go. I think care workers should help write the rules for care robots. Nobody asked us about the visit apps, and that went badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of you that's looking forward to this future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the night calls. If a robot could check on someone at three in the morning and call me only when it matters, that would save so much fear. I just don't want it doing the baths and the songs.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a real chance to involve **carers** and families.
I'd volunteer for a **council working group** if one existed.
think: Privately I'd be okay; robots around **2039** come when I'm 40.
Ten years is long enough to **change careers** twice if needed.
do: Buy the **flat** with Tom and pay a lot of it down.
Do the **dementia diploma** in a couple of years, without rushing.
Join any **carers' group** writing rules for care robots.
feel: **Hopeful** about robots covering frightening night calls.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning I'd still buy the flat, still do the diploma, and still sing the old songs with my clients.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets Esther go back to her **original plans**: flat, diploma, songs.
She wants carers to **write the rules**, citing the badly handled visit apps.
She sees robots as welcome for **night checks**, not for intimate care.

steps.text: Buy the flat near the hospital with Tom
Start the dementia specialist diploma within two years
Join a union or co-op group shaping care robot rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The AGI by 2028 one, because Tom and I would both be on the same three-year clock. What would help is a basic income that catches whole households, not just one person, and a guarantee that people with dementia can always ask for a human.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people who never had a family to come and visit. Robots might reach them first because nobody's there to say no. That's who I'd worry about most.

headlineQuote: What would help is a basic income that catches whole households, not just one person, and a guarantee that people with dementia can always ask for a human.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old co-op carer** who visits people with dementia for hour-long calls.
She's **steady** with technology, waiting for colleague Joanna to test tools before trying them.
Her mood turns **alarmed** in the fastest picture because partner **Tom's porter job** is hands-on too.
Her plans centre on a **dementia specialist** diploma and on the co-op controlling saved time.
She'd welcome robots for **night checks** but wants humans for baths and songs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, with both household incomes on the same clock.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that people with dementia can always ask for a **human carer**.
